title: Slides that start from a story

It started in group meetings, with slides that everyone could tell were made by AI, and with agents that turned two small edits into three copies of a deck. visibleText: Why I built it

title: My advisor can spot AI slides at a glance
pages.notes: This is where it started. In group meetings I see more and more slides made with AI, and I think that is the direction things are going: slides are data, a file format, so of course agents will learn to make them. But my advisor, and most people in the room, can tell at a glance when a deck was made by AI. Each tool has its own style, PowerPoint, Google Slides, ChatGPT, Kimi, and they all still look like AI. I read a post on Xiaohongshu that put it well: the AI look comes from having no focus, from covering everything, from having no story, from aiming to be complete and safe. Even this talk fell into it. On the right are pages from the previous version, made by Claude Code. They look fine. My comment on them was: the visuals are good, but there is no focus, because there is no story. That is the problem this project is about.

visibleText: My advisor can spot AI slides at a glance

In our group meetings, slides made with AI are becoming normal. Slides are data, a file format, so agents will learn to make them.

But my advisor, and most people in the room, can tell at a glance when a deck was made by AI. PowerPoint, Google Slides, ChatGPT and Kimi each have a style of their own, and all of them still look like AI.
Where the AI look comes from

•  No focus: every point gets the same weight
•  It covers everything instead of choosing
•  There is no story underneath
•  It aims to be complete and safe, not to say something
Even this talk

title: Two small edits should not leave three decks
pages.notes: The second problem appeared when I asked an agent to change a deck. Say I have fifty slides and want two of them fixed. Many agents are cautious: instead of replacing the file, they keep the original and write a new copy. One small tweak, another copy. After an afternoon the folder is full of near-identical decks, and the history is spread across file names. That made me think of Git. Version control works because the unit of change is small and every change is recorded. So in HUANDENG the page is the unit: an edit rewrites one page file and adds to that page's history, and a named version marks a milestone. The file names and edits here are an illustration, not a real folder.

title: Screenshots alone made agent edits slow to check
pages.notes: The third problem showed up when I asked AI to work on Google Slides or PowerPoint decks. To check its own work, the agent often had to render the whole slide to a picture, look at it, and work out from the pixels which value or position to change. Images can be measured and compared, but in that loop every precise fix had to be recovered from the picture first, and it was slow. So I wanted a slide format where the agent also reads the slide as data. On the right is a real excerpt from the 1BNA slide in this very project: the chart is an object with its bounds, its twelve values and its axis range. An agent can inspect and change one value or one label directly, without touching anything else, and the change can be diffed. I still look at renders for composition and readability; they are a review surface, not the editable model.

designIntent.purpose: Reason 3: screenshot-driven checks were slow and indirect; reading object values and bounds from the page file makes precise inspection and edits straightforward.

title: Start from the story, not from the slides
pages.notes: Here is the reason I care most about. If the AI makes the slides first, you then write a speech to fit them, and you end up following the AI's logic, which often has no soul. If you start by telling your story, freestyle, the way you would explain it to a colleague, the agent can organise that story, build the slides on it, and your own words become the speaker notes. Even improvised speech has a structure. Keeping it helps the deck keep your judgment and point of view, and you do not have to invent a script afterwards. It does not by itself remove an AI look: I still review the rendered pages. This talk is an example: I told the story of why I built HUANDENG, and this version was rebuilt from that account.

title: PPTD plus React, in a desktop editor
pages.notes: So what did I build? While looking at how people are teaching agents to make slides, I met the PPTD idea in the Kimi Slides ecosystem: a deck kept as a folder of page files rather than one packed file. Then I found OpenSlide, an open-source editor where every page is a React component. I thought these two ideas fit together: PPTD as the document, React as the interface. HUANDENG is that combination, packaged as an Electron desktop app. Most of the editing behaviour comes from OpenSlide; sections, views and notes borrow from PowerPoint and WPS, and the Layers panel takes its cue from Photoshop. Next to the editor sits a plugin, so that the AI client you already use can work in the same editor. Editor plus plugin is the workflow. To be precise about credit: OpenPPTD is a different project, and we reuse only its equation-conversion code. And HUANDENG has no affiliation with Kimi.

title: Unzip a PPTX: it is already pages
pages.notes: Here is the format idea in one picture. If you unzip a PowerPoint file, you find that it is already organised by page: presentation.xml, then slide1.xml, slide2.xml and so on, with media, notes and charts as separate parts. The left column comes from this deck's own exported PPTX. PPTD keeps the same idea but leaves the parts open as a working folder: deck.pptd for the order, one .page file per slide, a media folder, and a .huandeng folder for Slide IDs, Story, Sections, Presentations and history. So an agent can open one page file, and nothing forces it to rewrite the whole deck. HUANDENG still exports PPTX when you need to send it. This introduction is one such folder.

title: 1BNA: twelve base-pair distances, kept as data
pages.notes:
Here is the kind of slide this talk is about: one real result. The structure is PDB entry 1BNA, the Dickerson–Drew DNA dodecamer, drawn from its deposited coordinates; chain A is green, chain B ochre. For each of the twelve base pairs we measured the distance between the paired C1-prime atoms. The chart is not a pasted picture: it is a HUANDENG chart object holding the twelve values from the CSV, with a labelled axis that deliberately does not start at zero, so the geometric variation is visible. If a value or a label needs to change, you edit the data, not the pixels. Be careful about what the chart says: these are twelve positions in a single crystal structure. They are not replicates and carry no error bars. The shortest distance is at pair 7, a T–A pair in the central AATT region; the longest at pair 12, a terminal G–C pair.

Method: Euclidean distance between C1′ atoms, chain A residues 1–12 ascending paired with chain B residues 24–13 descending. Values from paired-c1-distances.csv (assets/science, generate.py).

Source: RCSB PDB 1BNA, https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1BNA; structure DOI 10.2210/pdb1BNA/pdb. Drew HR, Wing RM, Takano T, Broka C, Tanaka S, Itakura K, Dickerson RE. PNAS 78 (1981) 2179–2183, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.78.4.2179.

title: Story tells the agent what matters
pages.notes: This is the part of HUANDENG that comes most directly from the story-first idea. Every slide carries a short Story: what it is for, what must be kept, and what change was asked for. Think of it as an alignment tool between me and the agent. On the right is the Story actually recorded for the 1BNA slide: keep the exact values, keep the labelled axis and its units, keep the citation, and make no claims of replicates or trends. When an agent is asked to tidy that slide, it reads this first. Story also exists for the whole project, each Section and each Presentation. An agent's Story is its interpretation, not my approval.

title: Say “C014”, not “slide 4”
pages.notes: When I talk to an agent about my slides, I used to say: fix slide four. But if the order changed since the last version, slide four is a different slide. So HUANDENG separates the two. Position is just where a slide sits now. The Slide ID is a short four-character code, letters and numbers, that belongs to the slide for good. The status bar here shows Position moving from 2 to 4 while the Slide ID stays C014. Now I can say: fix the chart on C014, and the agent knows exactly which page I mean, next week as well as today. The same ID is what page history hangs on.

title: One Main library, two Presentations
pages.notes: A HUANDENG project has one Main Slides library. A Presentation is an ordered list of references into it. On the left is the project overview in the Editor, with the Main library and one Presentation. On the right is this very deck. The full introduction you are watching has twenty-five slides. The stacked previews and the grid are thumbnails rendered from this project's own export. Neither Presentation holds copies, so if I fix the 1BNA chart in Main Slides, both talks show the fix. The lab version gives four slides shorter speaker notes of their own; those notes belong to that appearance, not to the slide. visibleText: Working with agents

title: Agents work through the same writer as you
pages.notes: You keep the AI client you already use. Codex and Claude Code load the HUANDENG plugin locally over MCP; DeepSeek uses it through its Harness; ChatGPT reaches the local editor through a command-line route. Whatever the client, every write goes through the same shared writer that the editor window uses. The writer saves one transaction at a time and checks the revisions each request read. So several people and agents can work on one project: edits to different pages can both be saved, while a second edit to the same page, even to a different object, is refused if it was prepared from an older version. Story, Section and Presentation information shares one metadata revision, so those edits can conflict too. After a refusal, read the saved result and prepare a fresh preview. In 0.19 this was tested for real: a native DeepSeek Harness session and ChatGPT shared a three-page test project. Their independent page edits both survived, a stale same-page write was rejected once, and the following style handoff kept the other client's content. That run did not include a native Claude Code session, and it is not a claim of simultaneous raw file writes. There are no section locks, no automatic scheduling and no online presence: you agree who does what, and for a handoff you name the operation, the page and the revision. An agent's activity report is its own claim; the writer receipt is the record of what was saved. This version of the talk was written by Claude Code along this route.

title: Check, present and export
pages.notes: Before delivering, run Design check. It reads the whole collection and reports observations: type sizes outside the range you chose, unexpected backgrounds, Sections without a title slide, images with too few pixels for the size they are shown at. It is read-only; you still look at the slides yourself. Present starts from the beginning with F5 or from the current slide with Shift+F5, in a full-screen window with click builds. Export takes the slides as saved when it starts. The project folder itself is the editable source. PPTX keeps supported objects native, so a co-author can keep editing text, tables and basic charts in PowerPoint; animation becomes static. PDF is for sharing, and MP4 plays the click builds on a timer. This deck was exported to PDF and PPTX in exactly this way.

title: Built on open work, with clear gaps
pages.notes: HUANDENG did not start from nothing. The editor is built on OpenSlide, under the MIT licence. Equation conversion reuses code from the OpenPPTD repository; the GitHub mark here identifies that repository, it is not an OpenPPTD logo. PowerPoint export uses PptxGenJS. On the right are things HUANDENG does not do yet, as listed in the project README: importing arbitrary PPTX files and round-tripping them, editing Google Slides directly, a separate presenter window on a second screen, inheritable slide masters, native PowerPoint animation in exported files, and a plugin marketplace. If you need one of these, that is where a contribution would help most.

title: Start with your story
pages.notes: If you want to try it, open the editor and start a project, or open an existing one. You can open the .pptd file itself, or the project folder, as long as that folder directly contains exactly one .pptd; if it has none, or several, the Editor says so and asks you to choose the file. The folder is the project: pages, media and the .huandeng metadata live beside the .pptd, so copy or share the whole folder, not just the .pptd. Connect the AI client you already use from Agent setup. Then do what I did for this talk: tell the agent your story first, out loud and freestyle, and let it organise the story before it makes any slides. After that, ask for one change at a time, read the preview, apply it, and look at the review. The code and the build commands are on the right, and the repository is at the bottom. Thank you.
